stories.title_en: Using a Horse as Bait to Make Off with Silk

paragraphs.en: In Jiangxi there was a man surnamed Chen, given name Qing, who regularly dealt in horses, taking them to Nanjing to sell in front of Cheng'en Temple on Sanshan Street. At the time he had a fine silver-gray horse worth about forty taels. Suddenly a con man appeared, holding a fine umbrella and wearing showy clothes, sauntering up with an easy air. He stood there gazing at the horse, reluctant to tear himself away. Then he asked, "How much are you asking for this horse?" Qing said, "Forty taels." The con man said, "I'll buy it, but I have to go back home to draw up the deed and weigh out the silver." Qing asked, "Where do you live?" The con man said, "By Hongwu Gate." So the con man rode off on the silver-gray horse, with Qing following behind on another horse. Halfway there, the con man saw a silk shop. He dismounted, set his umbrella down beside a tavern, and told Qing, "Keep an eye on these for me while I buy a few bolts of silk; in a moment we'll go on together." Qing thought, "This man must be rich—the horse sale is as good as done." The con man went into the silk shop and deliberately haggled over the price. When the silk dealer scolded him for not knowing what the goods were worth, he pretended to relent: "Let me take it to a friend who knows the goods, and I'll come right back with an offer. How about that?" The silk dealer said, "With goods this fine, feel free to show them around—just don't go far." The con man said, "I have a horse and a partner right here—what is there to worry about?" He took the silk in hand, walked out the door, and ran off. The silk dealer, seeing the horse and the partner still there, felt perfectly at ease. Qing waited until noon; the man never came back, and Qing concluded he must be a swindler. So he left the umbrella, mounted the silver-gray, and led his other horse back toward the inn. The silk dealer rushed up and grabbed him: "Your partner made off with my silk—where do you think you're going?" Qing said, "What partner of mine?" The silk dealer said, "The man who rode here with you just now. Why play dumb? I'm taking it out of you." Qing said, "I don't know what devil that man was. He only asked to buy my horse and told me to come to his house to collect the silver, so I came along. He said he was buying silk at your shop and would rejoin me in a moment. I waited a long time and he never came, so I rode my own horse back to the inn. How can you harass me over nothing?" The silk dealer said, "If he wasn't your partner, why did he have you watch his umbrella and horse? I only handed him the silk because I saw you and the horse standing here. How can you two work a setup together and cheat me out of my silk?" The two of them argued, neither giving in, and hauled each other to the Yingtian prefectural office to have the case judged. The silk dealer told the whole story plainly. Qing pleaded, "I am registered in Jiangxi and deal in horses for a living. I regularly sell at Sanshan Street and put up at Weng Chun's inn. When have I ever been a swindler? I happened to meet a man who wanted to buy my horse and insisted I come to his house for payment, so I went with him. Midway he dismounted, took silk from this man's shop, and ran off—I knew nothing about it. How can you say I was his partner?" The prefect said, "Say no more. Bring in the innkeeper and all will be clear." The innkeeper said, "Qing regularly deals in horses and lodges at my place. He is an honest, law-abiding man." The silk dealer said, "If he's so honest, why did he watch the umbrella and horse for that swindler? I heard it plainly, and he agreed to it." Qing said, "He asked me to watch the umbrella because he was buying my horse—how does that make me his partner?" The prefect asked, "When the man left, did he take the umbrella?" The silk dealer said, "He did not." The prefect said, "Then he truly was a swindler. He wanted to make off with your silk, so he pretended to buy a horse and used Chen Qing as a pledge. Using another man's horse to trick you out of your silk—that is the 'borrow a path to destroy Guo' trick, using one thing as a pretext to take another. You fell for the swindle yourself; how can you blame Qing?" He dismissed them both without further testimony.

Note: Swindlers have many tricks. He spoke of buying a horse, but it was no horse purchase; what he really wanted was to use the horse as a decoy, a means of making off with silk. So first he dressed in showy clothes to make people believe he was truly rich; then he stood appraising the horse to make people believe he was a real connoisseur; then he entered the silk shop and lied about having a horse and a partner to make people believe his words were solid; and when he made off with the silk and ran, he left an umbrella with Qing so that Qing and the silk dealer would end up in court. All of it was clever trickery to make fools of people. Had the prefect not seen clearly and judged it a case of 'borrowing a path to destroy Guo,' then the passerby who picks up an ox would have become the townsman's calamity—the innocent bystander paying for another man's crime. Though Qing escaped being thrown into fetters, the silk dealer had already been bewitched in broad daylight. The petty man's schemes are crafty indeed; the gentleman's guard must be tight. Then, however many tricks swindlers have, they cannot make a fool of me.

In Tongzhou there was a man named Su Guang who, together with his son, dealt in Songjiang loom-woven cloth, taking it to Fujian to sell. With the silver from the cloth in hand, they were on their way back when they met a man named Ji Sheng, who said he was from the same prefecture but a different county—he spoke the same dialect—and was likewise returning from selling cloth in Fujian. Sheng was a green hand. On the road he claimed Guang as a fellow townsman, and seeing that Guang had the larger capital, he deposited twenty-odd taels of his own silver for safekeeping in Su Guang's chest. All along the way he was attentive and took on the chores, just like a traveling companion. But as the days wore on, Sheng saw the profit to be had and his mind turned crooked. One night he faked an upset stomach, getting up and opening the door to go out several times. He did not know that Guang was a seasoned traveler. Watching him open the door and go back and forth, Guang suspected a scheme; besides, the man's background was unclear. "True, he has twenty-odd taels deposited in my chest, but tonight he seems to be up to no good." Taking advantage of one of Sheng's trips out, Guang quietly got up, took his own silver together with Ji Sheng's silver and all the decent clothes and goods, hid them in another bundle, and kept it by his side. Then he wrapped several bricks and stones in the old clothes and bedding, put them back in the original chest, and pretended to be fast asleep. Sheng, seeing that Guang and his son were both asleep, shouldered Guang's silver chest and carried it off in the dead of night. In bed, Guang listened to Sheng's movements, and when Sheng went out and did not come back, he said, "So he really is a swindler. If it weren't for me, we'd nearly have been cleaned out." The next morning Guang got up and feigned shock that Sheng had stolen his capital; he seized the innkeeper and started beating him, accusing him of colluding to steal the silver. His son, not knowing his father's plan, was even more enraged and pummeled the man without letup. The father secretly told him, "I've already taken care of it, so-and-so." Only then did the son stop. After breakfast, Guang said, "I'm going to the county yamen to file a complaint. If they catch that swindler, you'll testify; otherwise I'll take it out of you." Guang knew that Sheng had fallen into his own trap, and he slipped straight home by a side road. Sheng, congratulating himself on stealing Guang's silver, trudged on in a daze until noon, nearly a hundred li down the road. He opened the chest: inside were bricks, stones, and old clothes. Stamping his feet in fury, he went back to the inn—where the innkeeper seized him and beat him, cursing, "You thief! You stole a man's silver and got me blamed for it!" He tied a rope around Sheng's neck and meant to haul him before the magistrate. Sheng had no choice but to spit out the whole truth and kowtow, begging to be spared. By then he and Guang were already several days' journey apart; there was no catching him, and Sheng could only stew in his own regret.

Note: Ji Sheng was no novice merchant—he was a novice swindler. First he deposited his own silver with Guang so Guang would not suspect; then he faked sickness to open the door, waited until they were sound asleep, and stole their silver along with his own and fled. His scheme was clever enough: this is 'give a little to take a lot,' a sweet trick in the swindler's repertoire. Who would have known that Guang was an old hand who saw one move ahead? Watching Sheng's comings and goings, he had already read him to the core. So he seized the moment and turned the scheme back on itself; Sheng had walked into his reckoning without ever knowing it. Sheng wanted to profit from another man's goods and ended up losing his own. A green sharp is no match for an old hand on the road. When he later returned to the inn, was seized and beaten, and had a rope twisted around his neck while he begged to be spared—he brought that misery on himself; who else is to blame? Heaven's justice is clear; let this serve as a warning.

Deng Zhaobao of Jianyang, Fujian, made his living as a porter-peddler. One day he was carrying four piglets to sell in Chong'an and Da'an. On Ma'an Ridge he met a con man who asked about buying pigs. Bao thought: this is a lonely mountain path, no one comes through, and the houses are far away—why would this man be buying pigs on the road? Suspicious, he asked where the man lived. The con man said, "Just ahead, at Ma'anping." Bao said, "If you mean to buy, I'll go home with you." The con man said, "I'm on my way to the county seat. Take one out for me to look at. If it suits me, we'll settle on a price and then I'll go home to weigh out the silver; otherwise I'm afraid it will delay my trip." The con man sounded reasonable, so Bao agreed and took out a pig to show him. The con man took it, held it by the tail, and set it on the ground to examine closely—then deliberately let go, and the pig bolted. Feigning alarm, he cried, "Oh no, oh no!" and rushed after it—though his chasing was really driving it farther away. Bao saw the pig running off and dashed forward with all his might to catch it, never realizing he had already fallen into the trap. When the con man saw Bao chasing the pig some two or three hundred paces from the cages, he turned back, grabbed a pig from a cage, kicked over the other two cages so the pigs all escaped, and shouted, "Much obliged! Take your time looking!" Bao wanted to chase the con man, but three pigs had bolted from the cages, and he feared losing them while chasing him; besides, the con man had gotten too far to catch. He could only curse him roundly. Luckily the three pigs bunched together; he gathered them back into the cages and went off nursing his grievance.

Note: Look how the swindler got away with the pig. In the space of a chance meeting, the thievish thought was born; he fooled Bao with lying words until Bao believed him completely—what is meant by 'a gentleman can be deceived by what seems plausible.' First he turned a pig loose and pretended to chase it, to draw Bao far off in pursuit; then he grabbed a pig and kicked over the cages, to keep Bao from coming after him: he made a man fall openly into the trap without ever knowing it. A setup thrown together on the spot—what cunning! Merchants, take warning from this. Do not think that only hidden snares and secret devices deserve careful guarding; even open traps and brazen setups demand still greater care.

stories.title_en: Meeting the Village Head, He Walks Off with a Teapot Instead

paragraphs.en: Zhao Tong was a man of Nanping County in Yanping Prefecture. His family had done good deeds for generations and held considerable tax-grain property, and by rotation he served as village head (lizhang) for the first tithing of the seventh ward. One of his tithing heads (jiashou), Lin Qianyi, was clever beyond most men but pursued no honest livelihood—he only drank, gambled, and visited prostitutes. In time his property dwindled away; with nowhere left to live, he had to flee the district, and Tong did not know where he had gone. One day Tong and his servant were traveling to Hangzhou on business. Passing through Pucheng, they stopped to rest at a pavilion, and there he caught sight of Qianyi. Tong lit into him: "You wretch! You've been on the run for years; the men of your household pay nothing, and I've had to cover the grain and service levies out of my own pocket. What do you call that? Now that you see me, what have you got to say for yourself?" Qianyi, stung by the scolding, hit on a plan. He stepped forward with an ingratiating smile: "I've always meant to come back and hand over the levy silver to you, village head, but my family owes people so much that I couldn't make it good, so I didn't dare return. Now meeting you here is like a gift from heaven—how could I put it off again? Besides, these past years, thanks to your blessing, I've opened a shop at the Xiguan wharf and my household is doing passably well. I recently married the concubine of a townsman named Xu, and some man has been forcing himself on her. I'm all alone out here, living by myself, and there's nothing I can do about it. Now that I've met you, village head, I have someone to stand up for me. On your way to Hangzhou you pass right by my door—stop and rest at my house a while, and of course I'll reckon up and repay the levy silver; and I'll trouble you to take my side." Hearing this, Tong rejoiced inwardly: "What I collect today can serve as travel money for Hangzhou. Truly, step out the door and wealth comes calling." So they went on together. At a tavern, Qianyi said, "Village head, you rose early this morning and have walked half the day; you must be hungry. How about we stop in and buy some wine to wet our mouths?" Tong answered, "Fine." They went in, and Qianyi called for the tavern keeper to warm wine and slice tofu for Tong to eat. Then he asked, "Do you have good red wine and pork here?" The tavern keeper said, "The You shop in front of the market has both meat and wine." Qianyi said, "May I borrow a pot and a scale?" The tavern keeper brought out a pot and scale; Qianyi took them, headed toward the You shop, turned corner after corner, and slipped away. Tong and his servant drank, and one pot was nearly gone when Tong said to the servant, "Qianyi's been gone a long time—could he have gotten into a fight? Otherwise he should be back by now. Go take a look." The servant went to the wine-and-meat shop to ask; they said there was no Qianyi there. He wanted to search but had no idea where the man had gone, so they could only weigh out silver to pay for the wine. The tavern keeper took the silver, then demanded the pot and scale. Tong said angrily, "I drank the wine, so paying you is fair enough; but you handed the pot and scale to Qianyi yourself—what has that to do with me?" The tavern keeper said, "The man came with you, and you were drinking in my shop—that's why I lent him the pot and scale. Otherwise, what do I know of any Qianyi?" Words flew back and forth, and the two fell into a shouting match. A crowd came to mediate and asked how it had started; only then did they learn that a tithing head had lured his village head into the shop and, into the bargain, walked off with the tavern keeper's pot and scale. Everyone laughed: "It was his own mistake—just pay the man and be done with it." Tong had no choice but to pay for them, and he left choking with resentment.

Note: Lin Qianyi began by saying his household was fairly comfortable, that his wife had been violated by some rogue, and that he wanted the village head to stand up for him—so that no one would suspect. Then he went into the shop and borrowed pot and scale to buy wine and meat, as if to renew an old friendship—so that no one was on guard. He played Tong like a toy in the palm of his hand; the trick was clever enough. Yet Qianyi's cunning was long-standing, and Tong knew it. Still, meeting him suddenly, Tong believed his words and went into the shop to drink; and the wish to buy red wine and meat was no true hospitality. Tong should have seen through the sham and stopped him: "The shop is inconvenient; if there's wine and meat, it won't be too late to eat it at your house." Then Qianyi's scheme would have had nowhere to go—he would have been too busy making his escape by the roadside. How would it ever have come to paying for a pot and scale and swallowing insults? So Qianyi was crafty—but Tong also failed to watch himself. Ah!

stories.title_en: Openly Stealing a Shop's Cloth Amid the Bustle

paragraphs.en: Wu Shengli, a man of Xiuning County in Huizhou Prefecture, ran a shop in Suzhou Prefecture buying up colored cloth of every kind. His wholesale business was the biggest around, buyers came from all quarters, and every day tens of taels of silver changed hands. The shop front opened to the street, and the goods were stored inside. One day several parties of customers crowded in to buy cloth, all of them in the inner hall settling accounts and weighing out silver. A swindler, taking advantage of the crush, also called out in the shop to buy cloth. Shengli came out to greet him politely, served him tea, and settled him in the outer shop to sit a while. Then Shengli went back inside to weigh out silver with the earlier customers. The swindler, seeing the shop unwatched, moved toward the doorway and pretended to cup his hands in a gesture of farewell; then he went to the edge of the shop, picked up a bundle of cloth, slung it over his shoulder, and strolled slowly away. Even the shop across the street did not see it as theft. Later, when the merchants in the inner hall had finished their dealings, Shengli saw his customers out—and suddenly found the bundle of cloth gone from the shop. He asked the people in the shop opposite, "Who took a bundle of cloth from my shop?" The people opposite said, "That customer who came later just now cupped his hands to take leave of you, then hauled the cloth off. We all saw it—why pretend you've lost cloth?" Shengli said, "Because I was busy inside, I seated him in the outer shop to wait until the earlier customers were done, and then I would settle accounts with him. When did I ever sell him cloth?" The neighbors marveled, "What a cunning swindler! He pretended to cup his hands in farewell so none of us dared call him a thief, and he strolled off and walked clean away with it in broad daylight. What can be done?" Shengli could only nurse his chagrin and let it go.

Note: When the swindler stole this cloth, he first had to take advantage of the crowd to get into the shop; he had not yet settled on how the swindle would play out. Only when Shengli served him tea and sat him down in the outer shop did he glance left and right—and then the crooked plan was fixed. So he cupped his hands in farewell and openly dragged off the cloth: like the sneak attack that took Jingzhou, it cost him hardly any effort. A real master of the game. As for Shengli, with goods piled up in the shop, he should never have left them unwatched; only so could he be sure of their safety. If the guard is not tight, how can you know no swindler will slip in and work his mischief? To wring your hands after the cloth is already lost—what good is that? All who keep shop should take this to heart and be careful.

stories.title_en: Pretending to Steal a Goose to Make Off with Blue Cloth

paragraphs.en: There was a big shop with bolts of cloth in great number and a constant press of business, and only the owner himself to mind the store. The people across the street kept a pen of geese whose honking was a constant racket. The shopkeeper hated the din and once said, "Why has no one stolen those wretched creatures? Then my ears could have some peace." A swindler happened to hear this. One day, finding the shop idle and quiet, he went in, cupped his hands, laid a hand on a bundle of blue cloth on the counter, and said softly, "I won't hide it from you—I'm really a petty thief. I'd love to make a meal of one of the geese at the shop across the way, but it's a busy street and hard to make a move. I have a little trick; I just need one person to play along." The shopkeeper said, "Play along how?" The thief said, "I'll stand here and ask, 'May I take it?' You answer loudly from inside, 'Yes.' I'll ask again, 'I'm really taking it?' You answer again, 'It's settled—take it as you please.' Then I'll go take it, and that will cover the eyes and ears of people in the street. Do me this favor, and afterward your house won't need to shut its door—no thief will ever enter. But you must stay inside; don't peek—if you look, the method won't work. Listen until the goose sounds stop; when my business is done, you can come out." The shopkeeper agreed. The thief asked loudly, "May I take it?" From inside came the loud answer, "Take it as you please." He asked again, louder, "I'm really taking it?" From inside again, "It's settled—take it as you please." The shops on both sides all heard this exchange. The thief then shouldered the bundle of blue cloth from the counter and walked off—people assumed it was a loan. Inside, the shopkeeper heard the geese still honking and dared not come out. The cloth thief had long since hurried away. He waited a good while; the honking never stopped. Fearing the shop had been left unwatched too long, he had to come out. He looked: the geese were still there—and a bundle of blue cloth was gone from his own counter. He turned to the neighboring shops: "Who was it just now came into my shop and took a bundle of my cloth?" The shops on either side all answered, "It was the one who asked to buy from you. You answered him again and again, telling him to go ahead and take it. He's been gone a long time." The shopkeeper beat his breast in remorse: "That man swindled me in broad daylight! And it's all my own doing—I can't even tell anyone." In time the neighbors figured it out; they laughed at the man's folly and deeply admired the swindler-thief's masterly skill.

Note: A gentleman is kind to people and cares for living things. Neighbors come first in kindness, and even geese count among the things to care for. What kind of care for living things is it, when a neighbor keeps geese, to hate their noise and wish a thief would make off with them and kill them? He counted the loss of his neighbor's geese a gain, and even helped the swindler-thief steal them—where was his humane heart? So when the swindler heard his words, seized the chance, and carried out his theft—and the man even abetted the stealing—he was a rat of the same nest. He wanted to be rid of another man's geese and lost his own cloth instead; he brought the misfortune on himself—whom can he blame? Had he treated his neighbor kindly and had the breadth of mind to tolerate things, he would never have suffered this loss.

stories.title_en: Borrowing Another Man's House to Make Off with a Customer's Cloth

paragraphs.en: Nie Daoying, also known by the name Xihu, was a man of Liudu in Shaowu. His family had once been wealthy, with a large, deep-set house. Later, lawsuits ate up the family fortune, and he made his living as a tailor. One day he went out to a customer's house to cut clothes. A smooth operator saw a cloth merchant selling cloth and, knowing Ying was out, led the man to Ying's house and seated him in the front hall. Then he went straight into the inner rooms and privately asked Ying's wife, "Is your husband home?" His wife said, "He's gone to the next village to cut clothes." The crook said, "I need several garments made. Will he be back today?" She answered, "Not until tomorrow." The crook said, "I have a companion sitting in your front hall who's thirsty. May I beg a cup of tea?" Ying's wife fetched two cups of tea and set them on the cutting bench. The crook carried the tea out to the cloth merchant. When the man had drunk, the crook took the cups back in, then came out, picked four bolts of cloth, and paid one tael of silver—but the silver was not pure. The merchant said, "At this price I need pure silver." The crook said, "My son is out cutting clothes for people; when he comes back tomorrow, I'll exchange it for you." Before he had finished speaking, a man the crook had planted in advance came and asked, "Is the tailor home?" The crook answered, "Not until tomorrow." The man left. The cloth merchant said, "Put the cloth away, then, and exchange it for me tomorrow." Once the merchant had gone, the crook a moment later hauled off the cloth and fled. The next morning the cloth merchant came to Ying's house and asked, "Is the tailor back?" Ying's wife said, "After noon." The following morning he asked again, "Is the tailor back?" Ying's wife said again, "Today at noon." In the afternoon the merchant came once more; Ying's wife said, "Not back yet." The merchant flared up: "The day before yesterday your father-in-law took four bolts of cloth, saying he'd pay the silver when the tailor came home. Why do you keep putting me off? Where has your father-in-law gone?" Ying's wife said, "What nonsense! What father-in-law do we have in this house? Who took your cloth?" The two fell into a shouting match. The neighbors reasoned with him: "When did this family ever have a father-in-law? Besides, her husband isn't home. We don't know who took your cloth—how can you demand it from them?" With no other recourse, the merchant filed a complaint with the vice prefect, Master Zhong. The complaint was accepted, and the neighbors on all four sides were summoned for questioning. They all said, "Ying was not home, and his father is long dead. We don't know who made off with the cloth." Master Zhong said, "The cloth was taken at his house. Who came to the house that day? Have the neighborhood elders investigate it thoroughly; there must be some trace." The neighborhood elders could find nothing, so they urged Xihu: "Your good wife should not have let the swindler wangle tea out of her, which misled the merchant into handing his cloth to him—you should bear half the loss. The merchant should not have handed his cloth to a stranger so lightly—he should bear half himself." Both households agreed and reported back accordingly. Master Zhong, finding the elders' settlement fair and clear, dismissed both parties without further testimony.

Note: When cloth is sold right into a man's house, and you drink the house's tea besides, the buyer seems to have a fixed address—who wouldn't hand over the cloth? Who would have thought this swindler borrowed the house and cadged the tea as a means to make off with the cloth—and even paid silver, quibbling only over its purity and promising to exchange it? Who would know to be on guard? From now on, in any deal, let both sides hand over on the spot. Even if he promises to exchange the silver, just carry the cloth back with you and return tomorrow—then you'll never be cheated out of your goods.

stories.title_en: Posing as a Carpenter to Make Off with a Money-Changer's Table

paragraphs.en: In Jianning Prefecture, the money-changers all set out a chair and a table-cabinet in the street, placed their coins on the table, and waited for people to come exchange. At noon they went home to eat; in the evening they gathered up the coins and left the table-cabinet with a household nearby. The next day, the same again. One changer had five or six thousand cash stored up in his table-cabinet, and the table had a broken corner. A swindler nearby, seeing how much money sat in that broken table-cabinet, hit on a plan. When the man got up to go eat lunch, the swindler dressed himself up as a carpenter—a towel tied around his waist, a sharp axe stuck at his side, a six-foot rule in his hand. He measured the table-cabinet lengthwise and crosswise, then said loudly, answering himself, "A thing this broken—they ought to have a new one made, and instead they tell me to patch it. How can this be patched? What a stingy man!" On and on he talked to himself. Then, rule in one hand, he gently tipped the coins in the cabinet over to one side, hoisted the table-cabinet onto his back, carried it to a deserted spot, chopped it open with the axe, took the coins, and ran. The bystanders all assumed the money-changer had called a carpenter to take it away for repair; who would have guessed that in the middle of a crowd a swindler would dare walk off with it? That afternoon the money-changer returned and asked the bystanders, "Where has my table-cabinet gone?" They all answered, "You had a carpenter take it for repair. The carpenter even said you were stingy—why not have a new one made instead of fixing that broken thing? He's already carried it off to fix." The money-changer said, "I never called any carpenter. A sharp has walked off with it." He hurried along the road asking after it, and found the table-cabinet split open in a deserted spot, not a single cash left. He went home sick with regret.

Note: This swindler came dressed as a carpenter, all big gestures and big talk—who would have known he was there to walk off with the goods? But a carpenter mending an old piece does the work in his own shop; why would he show up with an axe and a six-foot rule? Dressing up as a carpenter was itself the proof he was no carpenter. Still, it was another man's property and another man's repair job—who was going to cross-examine on his behalf? That is how the swindler got away with his fraud. And from this we can draw the general lesson: whenever a person's background is unclear and the act is all too convincing, watch him twice as carefully.
